usage: 책상 좀 저쪽으로 옮겨 주세요.
Please move the desk over there.
옮기다 = move an object from one spot to another; very common for furniture and boxes.
다음 달에 회사를 옮겨요.
I'm changing companies next month.
Also used figuratively: 회사를 옮기다 (change jobs), 자리를 옮기다 (change seats).
examples: 이사할 때 짐 옮기는 게 제일 힘들어요.
The hardest part of moving is carrying the stuff.
이사 (moving house) pairs naturally with 짐을 옮기다.
파일을 다른 폴더로 옮겼어요.
I moved the file to another folder.
Works for digital things too — files, data, photos.
무거우니까 같이 옮길까요?
It's heavy, shall we move it together?
같이 + 옮길까요? is a polite way to offer help.
nuance: 옮기다 is the everyday transitive verb for relocating an object — you physically pick it up and set it down somewhere else. It contrasts with 움직이다 (to move/budge in place) and 이사하다 (to move house). Koreans also use it figuratively for switching jobs, seats, or topics, so it is far broader than just lifting things.
mistakes: Don't confuse with 움직이다 — 움직이다 means something moves or budges, while 옮기다 means YOU move an object to a new location.
It's transitive, so you need an object: 짐을 옮겨요, not just 옮겨요 with no context.

usage: 의자를 끌지 말고 들어서 옮기세요.
Don't drag the chair, lift it to move it.
끌다 = drag along a surface; often discouraged because it makes noise or scratches floors.
저 가게가 사람들의 관심을 끌어요.
That shop draws people's attention.
관심을 끌다 / 인기를 끌다 = attract attention/popularity — a very common figurative use.
examples: 캐리어를 끌고 지하철역으로 갔어요.
I dragged my suitcase to the subway station.
Wheeled luggage is 끌고 가다 (pull-and-go).
강아지가 자꾸 줄을 끌어요.
The dog keeps pulling on the leash.
줄을 끌다 = pull a leash/rope.
회의 시간을 너무 끌지 마세요.
Don't drag the meeting out too long.
시간을 끌다 = to drag something out / stall — useful at work.
nuance: 끌다 covers dragging something along the ground (a suitcase, a chair) and, figuratively, drawing attention or dragging out time. It's a ㄹ-stem verb, so the ㄹ disappears before -ㅂ니다 and -세요: 끕니다, 끄세요. Note 끌다 (drag) is different from 끄다 (to turn off) even though their polite imperatives look similar.
mistakes: Don't write the formal form as '끌습니다' — the ㄹ drops, so it's 끕니다.
Don't mix up 끌다 (to drag/pull) with 끄다 (to turn off, e.g. 불을 꺼요). They share a 끄- imperative but mean different things.

usage: 쓰레기를 쓰레기통에 던졌어요.
I threw the trash into the bin.
던지다 = throw/toss an object through the air toward a target.
갑자기 질문을 던져서 당황했어요.
He suddenly threw a question at me and I was flustered.
질문을 던지다 = to pose/throw out a question — common figurative use.
examples: 공을 너무 세게 던지지 마세요.
Don't throw the ball too hard.
세게 (hard/forcefully) often modifies 던지다.
창밖으로 물건을 던지면 안 돼요.
You must not throw things out the window.
던지면 안 돼요 = it's not allowed to throw — a useful rule phrase.
저한테 열쇠 좀 던져 주세요.
Toss me the keys, please.
Casual request to throw something over; common among friends.
nuance: 던지다 is the standard verb for throwing or tossing something through the air. Beyond literal throwing, Koreans use it for 질문을 던지다 (pose a question) and 농담을 던지다 (crack a joke), where the idea is 'putting something out there.' For gently handing something over (not through the air), use 주다 or 건네다 instead.
mistakes: For handing something directly to someone, don't use 던지다 (it implies throwing) — use 주다 or 건네다.
The past tense is 던졌어요, not '던지었어요' — 지 + 었 contracts to 졌.

usage: 휴대폰을 바닥에 떨어뜨렸어요.
I dropped my phone on the floor.
떨어뜨리다 = cause something to fall; transitive partner of 떨어지다 (to fall).
조심하세요, 컵 떨어뜨리겠어요.
Be careful, you're about to drop the cup.
Warning use; -겠어요 here predicts an imminent accident.
examples: 지갑을 어디선가 떨어뜨린 것 같아요.
I think I dropped my wallet somewhere.
Common when you've lost something by dropping it.
계란을 떨어뜨려서 다 깨졌어요.
I dropped the eggs and they all broke.
Pairs with 깨지다 (to break) for fragile things.
서류를 떨어뜨리지 않게 잘 들고 가세요.
Carry the documents carefully so you don't drop them.
떨어뜨리지 않게 = so as not to drop.
nuance: 떨어뜨리다 is the causative/transitive form of 떨어지다 (to fall): you accidentally let something fall. Because the 'please don't' meaning (떨어뜨리지 마세요) is what you'd actually say, the polite imperative slot is rarely a positive command. Note it's also used figuratively for 점수를 떨어뜨리다 (to lower a score) and 고개를 떨어뜨리다 (to drop one's head/gaze).
mistakes: Don't confuse with 떨어지다 — 떨어지다 means something falls on its own; 떨어뜨리다 means YOU drop it.
Watch the spelling: 떨어뜨리다 (with 뜨) is the standard recommended form — 떨어트리다 is also accepted but stick with 떨어뜨리다.

usage: 출퇴근 시간을 피해서 가세요.
Go avoiding rush hour.
피해서 = avoiding ~; extremely common for dodging crowds, traffic, or busy times.
비를 피하려고 편의점에 들어갔어요.
I went into the convenience store to get out of the rain.
비를 피하다 = take shelter from rain; 피하다 covers escaping/avoiding a situation.
examples: 복잡한 길을 피해서 돌아갔어요.
I went around to avoid the crowded street.
피해서 돌아가다 = detour to avoid.
그 사람은 자꾸 제 눈을 피해요.
That person keeps avoiding eye contact with me.
눈을 피하다 = avoid someone's eyes/gaze.
사고를 피하려면 천천히 운전하세요.
Drive slowly to avoid an accident.
피하려면 = if you want to avoid ~.
nuance: 피하다 means to avoid, dodge, or steer clear of something — a person, a situation, bad weather, or a time of day. The construction N을/를 피해서 (avoiding N) is one of the most useful patterns for daily life in Korea, used for dodging rush hour, crowds, or the heat. It can be physical (dodging a car) or social (avoiding someone).
mistakes: Don't use 피하다 for 'miss/skip' an event — that's 빠지다 or 거르다. 피하다 is actively steering clear of something.
It's transitive: say 비를 피하다, 사람을 피하다 — include the thing being avoided.

english: to turn over, to flip, to hand over
usage: 다음 장으로 넘기세요.
Turn to the next page.
페이지/장을 넘기다 = turn a page; also swiping on a screen.
이 일은 다음 주로 넘겼어요.
I pushed this task to next week.
Figurative: 넘기다 = pass/postpone work or hand it off to someone else.
examples: 서류를 담당자에게 넘겼어요.
I handed the documents over to the person in charge.
넘기다 = hand over / pass responsibility.
사진을 옆으로 넘기면 다음 게 나와요.
Swipe sideways and the next photo shows up.
옆으로 넘기다 = swipe to the side on a phone.
힘든 시기를 잘 넘겼어요.
I got through the hard time okay.
시기를 넘기다 = get past/through a period — common figurative use.
nuance: 넘기다 is the transitive partner of 넘다 (to cross over): you make something go over or past. Practically it covers turning pages, swiping a screen, handing work off to someone, and getting through a tough period. It's very versatile — think 'pass it over / get it past.' For literally passing an object to someone's hand, 건네다 is more precise, but 넘기다 is common and natural.
mistakes: Don't confuse with 넘어지다 (to fall over/trip) — 넘기다 means to flip or hand something over, not to topple.
When handing something to a person, use the particle 에게/한테: 담당자에게 넘기다.

usage: 무거운 상자를 혼자 들어올렸어요.
I lifted the heavy box by myself.
들어올리다 = raise something up off the ground using your hands.
허리 다치지 않게 다리로 들어올리세요.
Lift with your legs so you don't hurt your back.
Practical safety phrasing for lifting heavy things.
examples: 이 짐 좀 같이 들어올려 주실래요?
Could you help me lift this load?
Polite request for help with heavy lifting.
아이를 번쩍 들어올렸어요.
I lifted the child right up.
번쩍 (in one swift motion) often pairs with 들어올리다.
바벨을 끝까지 들어올리지 못했어요.
I couldn't lift the barbell all the way up.
Common at the gym; 들어올리지 못하다 = fail to lift.
nuance: 들어올리다 is a compound of 들다 (to hold/lift) + 올리다 (to raise), emphasizing lifting something UP off a surface. Use it when the upward motion matters — heavy boxes, weights, a child. If you just mean 'hold/carry,' plain 들다 is enough; 들어올리다 specifically highlights the raising action.
mistakes: Don't overuse it where plain 들다 works — 가방을 들다 (carry a bag) is more natural than 들어올리다 unless you mean the upward lift specifically.
Written as one word: 들어올리다 (the spaced form 들어 올리다 is also seen, but keep it consistent).

english: to put down, to set down
usage: 짐을 여기에 내려놓으세요.
Put your bags down here.
내려놓다 = set something down from your hands/arms onto a surface.
이제 그 걱정은 좀 내려놓으세요.
Now let go of that worry.
Figurative: 마음을 내려놓다 / 걱정을 내려놓다 = let go, ease your mind.
examples: 무거우면 잠깐 내려놓고 쉬세요.
If it's heavy, set it down and rest for a bit.
Natural advice when someone is carrying a heavy load.
컵을 식탁에 살짝 내려놨어요.
I gently set the cup down on the table.
살짝 (gently) pairs well with 내려놓다.
짐을 아무 데나 내려놓지 마세요.
Don't just put your stuff down anywhere.
아무 데나 = just anywhere; common mild instruction.
nuance: 내려놓다 combines 내리다 (to bring down) + 놓다 (to place), meaning to lower something from your hands and set it down. It's the natural opposite of 들어올리다. Koreans also use it beautifully in a figurative sense — 마음을 내려놓다 means to let go of stress or attachment, much like 'putting down a burden.' Note 놓 is regular, so 내려놓아요 contracts to 내려놔요.
mistakes: The polite imperative is 내려놓으세요 (놓 keeps its ㅎ before 으세요), not '내려놔세요'.
Don't confuse with 놓다 alone — 내려놓다 adds the downward motion, ideal when lowering something you were holding up.

english: to flip over, to turn inside out
usage: 고기가 익으면 뒤집으세요.
Flip the meat when it's cooked.
뒤집다 = turn something over to its other side; essential for Korean BBQ and cooking.
빨래하기 전에 옷을 뒤집으세요.
Turn the clothes inside out before washing.
옷을 뒤집다 = turn clothing inside out — useful laundry tip.
examples: 전을 너무 일찍 뒤집으면 부서져요.
If you flip the jeon too early, it falls apart.
Cooking 전 (Korean pancakes) requires good timing to 뒤집다.
주머니를 뒤집어서 동전을 찾았어요.
I turned my pockets inside out to find coins.
주머니를 뒤집다 = turn pockets inside out.
그 소식이 분위기를 완전히 뒤집었어요.
That news completely flipped the mood.
Figurative: 뒤집다 = overturn/upend a situation.
nuance: 뒤집다 means to flip something to its other side or turn it inside out — flipping grilling meat, turning clothes for the wash, or upending a situation. Although it ends in ㅂ, it is a REGULAR verb (not a ㅂ-irregular), so it conjugates 뒤집어요, 뒤집습니다 — the ㅂ stays. For an item falling over on its own, use 뒤집히다 (passive) or 넘어지다 instead.
mistakes: This is NOT a ㅂ-irregular: it's 뒤집어요 / 뒤집습니다, never '뒤지워요'. The ㅂ stays put.
뒤집다 is transitive (you flip it); for something that flips/capsizes by itself, use the passive 뒤집히다.

english: to lean on, to rely on
usage: 벽에 기대지 마세요. 페인트 묻어요.
Don't lean on the wall, the paint comes off.
N에 기대다 = lean against a surface; the particle is 에.
힘들 때는 친구한테 기대도 돼요.
When it's hard, it's okay to lean on a friend.
Figurative: 사람에게 기대다 = rely on / lean on someone emotionally.
examples: 피곤해서 창문에 기대서 잤어요.
I was tired so I slept leaning against the window.
Very common on buses and subways in Korea.
벽에 기대 서 있는 사람이 누구예요?
Who's the person leaning against the wall?
기대 서다 = stand leaning.
너무 남한테 기대지 말고 스스로 해 보세요.
Don't rely on others too much; try doing it yourself.
기대지 말다 = don't rely/lean on.
nuance: 기대다 means to lean your body against something for support, and by extension to rely on someone. The particle is 에 for objects (벽에 기대다) and 에게/한테 for people (친구한테 기대다). It carries a warm nuance when emotional — 기대도 돼 ('you can lean on me') is a comforting thing to say. Don't confuse it with the homophone-ish 기대하다 (to expect/look forward to).
mistakes: Don't confuse 기대다 (to lean/rely) with 기대하다 (to expect). 기대돼요 = I'm excited/expecting; 기대요 = I lean on.
Use the particle 에 for surfaces: 벽에 기대다, not '벽을 기대다'.

usage: 몇 층 누르세요?
Which floor should I press?
Standard elevator question; 층을 누르다 = press a floor button.
이 버튼을 길게 누르세요.
Press and hold this button.
길게 누르다 = press-and-hold (long press) on a device.
examples: 벨을 눌렀는데 아무도 안 나와요.
I rang the bell but no one's coming.
벨을 누르다 = ring a doorbell / press a buzzer.
엘리베이터에서 닫힘 버튼을 눌렀어요.
I pressed the close button in the elevator.
닫힘/열림 버튼 = close/open button.
여기 좋아요 좀 눌러 주세요!
Please hit the like button here!
좋아요를 누르다 = tap 'like' — everyday social media phrasing.
nuance: 누르다 is the go-to verb for pressing or pushing buttons — elevators, doorbells, app icons, the 'like' button. It is a 르-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the stem becomes 눌ㄹ-, giving 눌러요 and 눌렀어요. Master this pattern because daily life in Korea is full of buttons to press, and getting 눌러요 right immediately sounds natural.
mistakes: This is a 르-irregular: the polite form is 눌러요 (not '누르어요'), and past is 눌렀어요.
For pushing a door or object (not a button), use 밀다; 누르다 is specifically pressing down on something.

english: to step aside, to get out of the way
usage: 죄송한데 잠깐만 비켜 주시겠어요?
Sorry, could you step aside for a moment?
비켜 주시겠어요? is the polite way to ask someone to move out of the way.
길 좀 비켜 주세요.
Please make way.
길을 비키다 = clear the path / step out of the way.
examples: 뒤에서 자전거가 와서 옆으로 비켰어요.
A bike came from behind so I stepped to the side.
옆으로 비키다 = move aside.
문 앞이니까 조금만 비켜 주세요.
You're in front of the door, please move a little.
Polite nudge to move; softer with 조금만.
사람들이 구급차를 위해 길을 비켰어요.
People cleared the way for the ambulance.
길을 비키다 for emergency vehicles.
nuance: 비키다 means to step aside or move out of someone's way. The polite request 비켜 주세요 / 비켜 주시겠어요? is essential for crowded subways, sidewalks, and elevators. On its own, a curt 비켜! is rude (like 'move it!'), so always soften it with 주세요 or 주시겠어요 unless you intend to be sharp. It's intransitive — you move yourself, not an object.
mistakes: Bare 비켜! sounds aggressive — always add 주세요/주시겠어요 to be polite in public.
비키다 is intransitive (you move aside); to move an OBJECT out of the way, use 치우다 or 옮기다.
